value: during exposure, wild-caught bank voles ranked the weasel-cue treatment as the greatest risk, with the rabbit and control treatments having similar ranks
units: rank of risk by proportion of millet harvested from a patch (rank 1 = greatest risk)
method: laboratory interview-chamber foraging trials: each vole interviewed for nine nights in systems of three sand-filled millet patches, each with a roof cue box holding weasel bedding (wood shavings, urine, hair and faeces), rabbit bedding (sham control) or nothing (control); 2-hour foraging round per night; proportion of millet harvested per patch compared by Friedman tests of concordance within chronological stages (pre-exposure, during exposure, post-exposure)
conditions: 39 analysed voles (40 trapped, 20 male and 20 female; one female removed for signs of pregnancy), trapped in forests around the Konnevesi Research Station and near Oulainen (Finland) and held a few weeks in the laboratory; food withdrawn four days before the experiment; cue boxes 11 x 11 x 6 cm with fresh bedding daily, no dose or mass stated and the paper does not say whether weasel or rabbit bedding came from wild or captive animals; treatments randomised in system and hour of interview; during-exposure nights a live least weasel was caged beside one room of two systems expanded to four rooms, so the ranking is under live predator presence, not bedding odour alone

source.authors: Bleicher SS, Ylönen H, Käpylä T, Haapakoski M
source.title: Olfactory cues and the value of information: voles interpret cues based on recent predator encounters

quote: During the exposure, the voles ranked the weasel-cue treatment as the greatest risk with the rabbit and controls having similar ranks.
note: Classification: behavioural response (foraging patch use) of wild-caught voles to predator-bedding odour in the presence of a live caged predator; no chemoreceptor is identified and no odour-only effect is shown for the exposure stage. Test statistics for this stage (Table 1): Friedman chi-square 6.764, df 2, P = 0.034, Kendall W = 0.087. Contrary and secondary results from the same paper: Friedman tests found no main effect of cue treatment on foraging tenacity (chi-square 3.273, P = 0.195, W = 0.042) while chronology (P < 0.001) and the chronology x treatment interaction (P < 0.001) were significant; concordance in risk assessment was found only during and post exposure (the sentence before this one in the paragraph), not pre-exposure; post-exposure voles ranked the control least dangerous and avoided rabbit and weasel cues similarly; vole activity was lower in all patch types when the live weasel was present and activity in rabbit (sham) patches was highest on exposure nights; mean rank 1.31 during exposure versus 2.46 pre-exposure and 2.23 post-exposure (the paper's wording: the lower the rank the greater the risk; the Methods do not define rank); males harvested less overall than females (16.7% vs 21.9%); mean harvest in control patches rose from 19.4% to 30.1% after exposure. The quote prints no comma between 'risk' and 'with' (reader confirmed). The effect is small (W = 0.087).
